subject: physics

items.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by a key idea in physics?
items.correct: An idea that runs through many topics and describes a wide range of phenomena
items.misconception: A rule that applies only inside the particular topic in which it is first taught
items.why: Teaching, revision guides and exam papers are organised topic by topic, so the connections between topics are easy to miss. The same small number of key ideas runs through every topic. 'Differences drive change', for example, explains fluid flow, heating and electric current alike.
items.random_wrong: A detailed description of one particular phenomenon in great depth

items.q: Energy is transferred from a hot drink to a cooler room, and charge flows through a lamp connected to a cell. Which key idea links these two examples?
items.correct: A difference between two places is what drives the change
items.misconception: A large store always empties into a store that is smaller
items.why: Students merge the ideas of temperature and stored energy, so the bigger or heavier object is assumed to heat the smaller one. The driver is the temperature difference, not the amount stored. A small hot block heats a large cool tank, even though the tank's store of energy is far greater.
items.random_wrong: Both are examples of action at a distance through a field

items.q: Which of these is listed in the specification as a key idea in physics?
items.correct: That differences, such as those between temperatures, drive change
items.misconception: That each separate area of physics is governed by its own set of rules
items.why: Teaching, revision guides and exam papers are organised topic by topic, so the connections between topics are easy to miss. The same small number of key ideas runs through every topic. 'Differences drive change', for example, explains fluid flow, heating and electric current alike.
items.random_wrong: That background ideas are read about but are never actually assessed

items.q: How do the key ideas relate to the assessment of GCSE Physics?
items.correct: They are embedded in the content and assessed across all papers
items.misconception: They are background information and are never assessed in the exam
items.why: The key ideas are not written as a separate teaching topic with its own recall content, so they look like preamble. Because they are embedded throughout the subject content, they are assessed through the topics themselves, on every paper rather than in one place.
items.random_wrong: Each key idea is assessed only within the topic that it belongs to

items.q: Why do scientists use a model such as the particle model of matter?
items.correct: It gives a simplified description that explains and predicts behaviour
items.misconception: It is a scaled-down physical copy of the material being studied
items.why: In everyday language a 'model' is a scaled-down object, and the first models students meet in school are often physical demonstrations. In physics a model is a way of representing how something behaves. The particle model and the wave models of light and of sound are ideas, not objects, and they earn their place by explaining and predicting behaviour.
items.random_wrong: It shows precisely what the particles themselves really look like

items.q: A model of matter treats particles as tiny solid spheres, although real particles are not solid spheres. What does this tell you about the model?
items.correct: It can still be useful even though it is not a true picture
items.misconception: It is wrong, and so it should no longer be used in physics
items.why: Students treat scientific statements as simply true or false, so 'not completely accurate' is read as 'false'. Models are judged by usefulness, not by whether they are complete. A model is used within the range where it explains and predicts well, and a different model is used beyond it.
items.random_wrong: It must be a physical copy of the material it represents

items.q: The specification gives 'the wave models of light and of sound' as an example of which key idea?
items.correct: The use of models to describe and explain phenomena
items.misconception: The idea that forces act only through direct contact
items.why: Everyday experience of pushing and pulling is entirely by contact, so a non-contact force feels as though it needs a physical link. ‘Action at a distance’ is a real phenomenon, and it is analysed using the concept of the field: the object produces a field, and a second object placed in that field experiences a force.
items.random_wrong: The idea that all relationships in physics are linear

items.q: A resultant force acts on an object and the object accelerates. Which statement describes the cause and the effect correctly?
items.correct: The resultant force is the cause; the acceleration is the effect
items.misconception: The acceleration is the cause; the resultant force is the effect
items.why: Force and acceleration are always seen together and are related by a single equation, so students reverse the direction of the explanation. The resultant force acts on the object and the object responds by accelerating: force = mass × acceleration, F = m a. The equation gives the size of the effect, while the force remains the cause.
items.random_wrong: Neither causes the other; they simply occur at the same moment

items.q: A nucleus of an unstable atom changes and a radioactive emission is detected. Which statement applies the key idea of cause and effect?
items.correct: The change in the nucleus causes the emission that is detected
items.misconception: The emission being detected is what makes the nucleus change
items.why: Force and acceleration are always seen together and are related by a single equation, so students reverse the direction of the explanation. The resultant force acts on the object and the object responds by accelerating: force = mass × acceleration, F = m a. The equation gives the size of the effect, while the force remains the cause.
items.random_wrong: The two events are linked only because they occur together

items.q: A magnet attracts a steel paperclip without touching it. Which key idea does this illustrate?
items.correct: Action at a distance, explained using the idea of a field
items.misconception: Contact forces, because the air must touch the paperclip
items.why: Everyday experience of pushing and pulling is entirely by contact, so a non-contact force feels as though it needs a physical link. ‘Action at a distance’ is a real phenomenon, and it is analysed using the concept of the field: the object produces a field, and a second object placed in that field experiences a force.
items.random_wrong: Fields, but only once the paperclip is brought up close

items.q: Which statement best describes what is meant by a field in physics?
items.correct: A region in which an object experiences a non-contact force
items.misconception: A region that forms only once a second object is placed close by
items.why: The field is only ever detected by its effect on something else, so students conclude that the second object is what creates it. The second object reveals the field; it does not create it. A magnet has a magnetic field around it even with nothing nearby, just as a planet has a gravitational field.
items.random_wrong: The surface where two objects make contact and push one another apart

items.q: A small hot metal block is placed in a large tank of cooler water. What determines the direction of the energy transfer by heating?
items.correct: The difference in temperature between the block and the water
items.misconception: Which of the two objects stores the greater amount of energy
items.why: Students merge the ideas of temperature and stored energy, so the bigger or heavier object is assumed to heat the smaller one. The driver is the temperature difference, not the amount stored. A small hot block heats a large cool tank, even though the tank's store of energy is far greater.
items.random_wrong: How hot the block is, whatever the water's temperature may be

items.q: Air rushes out of an inflated balloon when its neck is opened. What drives this flow?
items.correct: The difference in pressure between the inside and the outside
items.misconception: The high pressure of the air inside the balloon, on its own
items.why: Everyday phrasing refers to a single value ('high pressure', 'the voltage here'), which hides the fact that two points are always being compared. Nothing flows when both places are the same, however large the value. Air flows only when the pressures differ, energy is transferred by heating only when the temperatures differ, and charge flows only when there is a potential difference.
items.random_wrong: The greater quantity of air that is stored inside the balloon

items.q: A graph of weight against mass for several objects is a straight line through the origin. What does this show?
items.correct: Weight is directly proportional to the mass of the object
items.misconception: Gravitational field strength rises as the mass increases
items.why: Students treat every symbol in an equation as a variable, and do not distinguish the constant of proportionality from the quantities it relates. In force = spring constant × extension, F = k e, the value of k is fixed for a given spring. That is exactly what makes force and extension directly proportional.
items.random_wrong: Weight and mass are the same quantity in different units

items.q: What must a graph show if two quantities are to be directly proportional?
items.correct: A straight line that passes through the origin
items.misconception: A straight line, wherever it happens to cross an axis
items.why: 'Linear' and 'proportional' are used loosely in conversation, and most straight lines students plot happen to go through the origin. A straight line that cuts an axis away from the origin shows a constant rate of change but not proportionality, because doubling one quantity does not double the other.
items.random_wrong: A line whose gradient increases steadily as it rises

items.q: A spring extends 40 mm when a force of 8.0 N is applied. Force and extension remain directly proportional. What is the extension when the force is 12 N?
items.correct: 60 mm
items.misconception: 27 mm
items.why: Students treat every symbol in an equation as a variable, and do not distinguish the constant of proportionality from the quantities it relates. In force = spring constant × extension, F = k e, the value of k is fixed for a given spring. That is exactly what makes force and extension directly proportional.

items.q: What does it mean to say that a physical law is expressed in mathematical form?
items.correct: The relationship between the quantities is written as an equation
items.misconception: The symbols are shorthand labels and carry no relationship
items.why: Equations are most often met in calculation questions, so their role in stating a relationship goes unnoticed. Physical laws and models are expressed in mathematical form. F = m a says that acceleration is proportional to resultant force for a fixed mass — a statement about the world, before any number is substituted.
items.random_wrong: The equation works only in the exact order it is written

items.q: The equation F = m a is rearranged to a = F ÷ m. What effect does this rearrangement have?
items.correct: None; it states the same relationship in a different form
items.misconception: It changes the relationship so acceleration now causes force
items.why: The subject of the equation looks like the thing being 'produced', so moving it appears to move the cause. F = m a and a = F ÷ m are the same statement. Which form is used depends on which quantity is being calculated; it says nothing about which quantity is the cause.
items.random_wrong: It makes the symbols stand for different physical quantities

items.q: Does the particle model show what particles really look like?
items.correct: No. The model represents particles in a simplified way in order to explain behaviour; it is not a picture of what particles actually are.
items.misconception: Particles really are tiny solid coloured spheres, because that is how the model draws them.
items.why: Diagrams and animations always draw particles as identical spheres, and students take the representation for the reality. The spheres are a representation chosen because it makes arrangement and movement easy to reason about. The usefulness of the model does not depend on particles looking like that.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Two quantities change together. Does one cause the other?
items.correct: Not necessarily. Things that happen together may both be caused by something else, or may be unconnected.
items.misconception: If two things always happen at the same time, one of them must be causing the other.
items.why: Students meet cause and effect mainly through examples where the link is real, so they treat any association as proof of a cause. A causal claim needs a mechanism, not just an association. The specification's examples work because there is a physical mechanism: a resultant force acting on a mass produces acceleration, and a change in a nucleus produces an emission.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are weight and mass the same thing?
items.correct: No. They are different quantities, related by weight = mass × gravitational field strength, W = m g.
items.misconception: Weight and mass are the same quantity, just written in different units.
items.why: The two words are used interchangeably in everyday life, and on Earth weight is always the same fixed multiple of mass. Mass is measured in kilograms and weight is a force measured in newtons. They are directly proportional at a given place, which is why the confusion survives, but they are not the same quantity.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.9 Key ideas
